meta.title: My thoughts on Gas Town after 10,000 hours of Claude Code
meta.author: deevus

comments.author: doctor_eval
comments.text:
I just refuse to consider vibecoding as “vibe engineering”.

I consider engineering to the the application of scientific principles to the development of an artefact. This is no such thing. It’s not remotely scientific. It’s in the name!

This is not a value judgement. Writing a novel is not generally considered engineering, either. But Vibecoding by definition does not care how it’s done, and engineering, by most reasonable definitions, does.

Related,


I’ve never seen the code, and I never care to, which might give you pause. - Steve Yegge


I feel like there is going to be a reckoning in a year or two where all the shocking security shortcuts and lack of care that I’ve witnessed from Claude Code start to find their way into malign hands. If it hasn’t already.

comments.author: deevus
comments.text:
Are you referring specifically to Gas Town, or agentic code generation in general?

The way I use Claude Code, I am using engineering principles, I’m just not writing 100% of the code. I guess what I’m saying is don’t throw out the baby with the bath water.

comments.author: doctor_eval
comments.text:
Mostly Gas Town.

I think Claude assisted coding is still engineering, as long as an engineer is still making decisions and all code is reviewed. I use Claude myself and it has made me more productive on some tasks, especially smaller changes, but I’ve learned to pick and choose what I get it to do.

But that’s not vibecoding, which as I understand it is epitomised by Yegge’s comment that he’s “never seen the code”.

Frankly, I think it’s absolutely irresponsible to publish a product with code you’ve never read. My guess is that it’s all going to come crashing down on folks. Especially people who are pushing out production code based on this stuff.

LLMs are amazing technology, but the problem has never been writing the code, but understanding what needs to be done. If you spend just as much time writing English as you do writing code, I’m not sure what the benefit is.

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text:
I consider engineering to the the application of scientific principles to the development of an artefact.


So far some of the problems in software can be neatly tracked by how people start applying natural science principles to deal with what was supposed to be designed — but what can only be studied experimentally nowadays. Code sight-unseen development might soon get to satisfy your definition of engineering too, and we won't like it.

comments.author: doctor_eval
comments.text:
I think you're saying that many problems with computing come from an attempt to fit requirements into "scientific" boxes, but that's not really my position - I certainly agree that requirements gathering is one of the hardest problems in computing, and possibly even somewhere that LLMs can help. But in any case, that's squishy social stuff that's also true in other engineering fields.

My position is more that software engineering - developing and deploying the actual code - is about applying principles from logic, discrete maths, computer science, etc to write code. Like, if you need to search for something, you can select from a number of algorithms with various O and constant time properties depending on the actual problem. That's what I think of as engineering, and that's the sort of analysis that LLMs don't seem to do very well.

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text:
I am claiming a worse thing. I am claiming that we have let the sets of requirements to be of size and type where


about applying principles from logic, discrete maths, computer science, etc to write code


has hit the reality of «and now test your underlying layer, and see that it lies about what it does»,

If I ask when adding an instruction makes the hot loop run faster, will the answer lie in carefully reading the manual, or in a benchmark? If I ask what a weird combo of flags does on Windows, will you believe an interpretation of documentation, or a test? If I ask which open-source terminals do what with Unicode width, will the answer come from source code reading, or from running a test script?

But also, how many more decades until we have a fighting chance to calculate best metal ratios in centuries-old alloys for a given use?

I guess we will be able to fit running-code-sight-unseen into the paradigm of «treat this as external reality, and run experiments on it». I guess it will not do any good neither to reliability nor to flexibility (short of rewriting) of software produced. But it's not like reliability has recently been priority in software requirements as observed via development processes, not marketing talk…

comments.author: mitchellh
comments.text:
I always view new ideas from the PoV of good faith and optimism. My first reaction, even artificially, is usually "super cool" and then "why is this going to be a good thing?" And then I get more critical from there. I'm a default-from-positivity type of person. I think too many technologists are pessimistic or dismissive by default. As a way of disclaimer, I'm also someone who productively and happily uses AI in my everyday life, including coding.

Despite all of the above, I will not use Gas Town. I don't find it trustworthy (on its OWN code basis, not even considering what it does). Beads is filled with questionable unsafe code paths.

But, I'm still an optimist! So how does that apply here...

Well, I think all things come with nuance. I don't believe an idea like Gas Town is going to replace engineering at large in most forms (if any) in the next 5 years even.

But, things like Gas Town (also colloquially referred to more generally as slop engineering, Ralph loops, etc.) have their place. I would MUCH rather some engineer ship a PoC of a product or feature using slop like Gas Town in a day spending hundreds of dollars than even the same amount of time (but likely more) on a standard Silicon Valley engineering salary.

Or, another point of view: agent orchestration is a huge challenge right now even for well-constrained problems where agents do really well. I highly highly predict this will be solved by the end of the year by all the major agentic programming providers. Gas Town is a [Wild West] approach to agent orchestration. Note when I say "agent orchestration", I mean basically a controlled Ralph loop: human aided design followed by "paint the owl" distributed over multiple agentic sessions, with control points where the AI/human can reconverge to verify its on the right path, rinse and repeat.

And that's where the idea is exciting and worth looking at seriously. I'm not a fan of throwing out the baby with the bathwater, so to speak. You can find something you personally find awful and still study it, play devil's advocate, learn from it, and find portions of it you can appreciate.

I still won't use Gas Town. :)

comments.author: mxey

Where new databases come out and think hopes and prayers are a replacement for fsync. I spend so much time at work finding failures and design flaws in software just because I ask some basic questions about it.

comments.author: spc476
comments.text: I once had a PoC put into production without my knowledge.  It's incidents like these over the course of a career that can turn optimists into pessimists.

comments.author: deevus
comments.text:
Me too, with regards to the good faith and optimism. I relish the moments when I discover a cool new tool that I can try out! Being a Zig fanboy, I was waiting with baited breath for Ghostty to be available for me to try.

So when beads was dropped, I jumped in and started seeing good results with it. As I mentioned in the article it just doesn't gel with the way I like to work. I'm just not comfortable with deploying code sight unseen. If storing AI metadata in version control is the way, our code review tools need to get better. Perhaps there is a market for human focused code review tools that automatically hide the AI cruft that is not important, and is safe to ignore.

I am still worried about the "erosion of expertise" as I like to call it. Where will we be in 10-20 years if the only entities that understand the fundamentals of software are AI agents?

comments.author: thesnarky1
comments.text:
Even if I am vibe engineering, I still care about the code. I still look at it. I think Gas Town is cool, but I don’t think it’s for me, yet.


There's something else that bothers me about this, more than just not seeing the code (which I care about). This quote from the original (whose sentiment is manifested in a few places):


Yuck! Nobody cares, I know. You want to get stuff done, superhumanly fast, gated only by your token-slurping velocity. Let’s talk about how.


The "token-slurping" velocity seems to be the future many want to go to. While we say "AI is letting people learn how to program," the reality is the intended future is entirely money-based. More money goes in, more code comes out. It is pay to play. In that end-state, no one learns how to program because learning how to write code doesn't give the the velocity you need, it is all about becoming an entrepreneurs, getting enough wealth to kick-start the process, and watching it unfold.

Further, as much as the Internet is ingrained in our society now, it will become a requirement for any company to get work done. There is no code unless your high-speed line over to the AI provider is up. No coding while riding the bus, no waking up after a dream and grabbing your pen to jot something down, forget about doing anything off a hotspot unless you're just connecting to your VPS that still has a pipe to your AI provider.

Whether or not that is the future, it makes me incredibly sad that we would even desire such an endstate. Knowing what it will do to the already significant divide between the haves and the have nots. Maybe instead we should be planning for how to produce good, quality code, on D+1 after the VC money runs out and these plans come crashing down.

comments.author: rau
comments.text:
That’s where my issue with Gas Town lies. It feels like deferring everything to agents, and I get almost no visibility of what’s going on other than work was completed. Don’t get me wrong, I understand that I can ask the mayor to explain what was done, or link me to the code in question, though it feels very cumbersome.



Additionally, with the token speed of current agents (Claude Opus 4.5 in my case), unless you have many rigs operating at once, the whole process just seems really slow. Since I like to be more involved, it just feels like I’m sitting there forever waiting for things to happen.


The lack of visibility, the cumbersome nature of oversight and the slow cycle time are exactly the sort of complaints anyone who delegates to human beings will have.

It would be funny/worthwhile if deploying teams of agents to solve problems is the thing which gives line workers some sympathy and empathy for corporate managers.  It’s tough managing people or agents, but it’s also necessary in order to achieve anything larger than a single man or machine can achieve.

comments.author: rvt
comments.text:
I keep saying a lot of the agentic trends right now is humans figuring stuff out. None of it needs to be accepted as canon, and we can all take it as an interesting exploration of constraints (one of them being $$ to spin up lots of Claudes).

Opinion is good. The unfortunate thing is when BigCo et al. drop <Product Name / Protocol> and folks adopting it assuming it's a linear progression / improvement on past things. Instead we're very much in a breadth-first exploration state now IMO.

comments.author: DanOpcode
comments.text:
Sounds like a fun program to try.

But I wonder how does the author use Claude Code for pair programming? Would be interesting with some more description of that workflow

comments.author: deevus
comments.text:
I alluded to that in this post: https://simonhartcher.com/posts/2025-12-31-give-your-agentic-processes-a-name/

Short version:


Try using the brainstorming skill from https://github.com/obra/superpowers . This gives you way more insight into what is going to be delivered. The agent does all the coding while you watch and comment. With the executing-plans skill it will stop for feedback after each batch of tasks.

Use the above with what I've called "test driven pair programming". Agent writes the tests, you write the implementation. This is very fun!
